lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Diogenes — did you know Moerichus? The rich one. The really rich one. From Corinth. The one with all the merchant ships. His cousin was Aristeas — also rich. The one who was always quoting that line from Homer: 'Either you lift me, or I'll lift you.'
lines.description: warm storyteller, setting up gossip with dry relish

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Well — they were buttering each other up for the inheritance. Both the same age, you see. They'd each filed their wills publicly. Moerichus left everything to Aristeas if he died first; Aristeas left everything to Moerichus if he went first. That part was in writing. After that it was a competition in flattery — who could be more obsequious. And the prophets got involved too — the astrologers, the dream-readers, the whole Chaldean crowd — and even Apollo himself at Delphi kept switching: one day Aristeas had the edge, next day Moerichus. The scales tipped one way, then the other.
lines.description: expansive raconteur, amused by each absurd escalation

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And how did it end, Crates? This I want to hear.
lines.description: leaning in, sharp appetite for the verdict

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: They died on the same day. Both inheritances went to Eunomius and Thrasycles — relatives, neither of whom had ever seen this coming. They were sailing across from Sicyon to Cirrha, got broadsided by the Iapyx wind mid-crossing, and went under.
lines.description: matter-of-fact punchline, pleased but not gloating

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Good for them. [pause] You and I, when we were alive — we never had thoughts like that about each other. I never once prayed for Antisthenes to die so I could inherit his stick — and it was a very good stick, mind you, wild-olive, he'd made it himself — and I don't suppose you, Crates, were lying awake hoping to inherit my estate after I died: the jar, the satchel, and the two quarts of lupin beans.
lines.description: dry approval, then scornful reminiscence with tiny pride in poverty

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: I had no need of any of it. Neither did you, Diogenes. The things that mattered — those you inherited from Antisthenes, and I inherited from you. Far greater and grander than the Persian Empire.
lines.description: sincere warmth, quietly grand but still Cynic-dry

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Wisdom. Self-sufficiency. Truth. Plain speech. Freedom.
lines.description: simple, deliberate list; let each word carry weight

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: By Zeus, yes — I remember now. I took the whole fortune over from Antisthenes, and left you an even bigger one.
lines.description: mock revelation, gruff affection under the joke

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: But nobody else cared about that sort of property. Nobody fawned on us hoping to be in the will. They were all watching the gold.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Naturally. They had nowhere to put what we had. They'd rotted through with luxury — like old purses with the bottom worn out. Drop wisdom into them, or plain speech, or truth, and it'd fall straight out the bottom: nothing to hold it in. Like those daughters of Danaus, pouring water into the leaky jar. But gold — that they kept hold of with teeth, nails, and every trick they had.
lines.description: acidly precise, building from image to contemptuous verdict

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Well — we'll still have our wealth down here. They'll arrive with one obol, and even that goes straight to the ferryman.
lines.description: cheerful final sting, friendly and deadpan
